messages.author: fc7cc12862219cdf
messages.subject: Heterogeneous camera trapping data
parts:
Hello,

I work on SCR analysis to estimate Balkan lynx density in North Macedonia. I have four sessions of camera trapping over the same period but with very heterogenous results:

-        2013 : 33 recaptures / 9 individuals

-        2015 : 17 recaptures / 8 individuals

-        2018 : 31 recaptures / 10 individuals

-        2021 : 8 recaptures / 4 individuals

I know I don’t have enough individuals and/or recaptures on some years (2015, 2021) to do a single session analysis. Moreover closure.test indicate an open area for 2013 : 3 lynx captured only once, one lynx twice but only one of them never recaptured. 

My question is : does a multi-season model allow me to use those years where there is less data? Any idea not to “lose” those years ?

I hope the answer is not so obvious and not just no …

Thank you in advance !

Yon

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: Heterogeneous camera trapping data
parts:
A multisession analysis allows you to fit a model with each detection parameter (g0 or lambda0 and sigma) held at the same value across years (e.g. g0~1, sigma~1). If that is a reasonable assumption (I expect it is) then there is no reason to 'lose' any data. It's worth also checking by AIC whether there is clear evidence for annual variation in density (D~session vs D~1). The 'heterogeneity' you see may just be sampling variation (although I expect not).
Murray

parts:
Hello and thank you Murray,

I managed to run hybrid mixture models with the sex partially known. 
But now I doubt about the choice of the best detection model. Here the AIC comparisons, first with constant density :
> AIC(null, sig0.sex, sig.sex, g0.sex)
                    model             detectfn     npar  logLik       AIC      AICc     dAICc   AICcwt
g0.sex    D~1 g0~h2 sigma~1 pmix~h2   halfnormal    5   -421.0881   852.176    855.033   0.000   0.4415
sig.sex   D~1 g0~1 sigma~h2 pmix~h2    halfnormal    5   -421.4123   852.825   855.682   0.649   0.3192
sig0.sex D~1 g0~h2 sigma~h2 pmix~h2    halfnormal    6   -420.6948   853.390   857.590   2.557   0.1230
null       D~1 g0~1 sigma~1 pmix~h2   halfnormal    4   -423.9416   855.883   857.701   2.668   0.1163

And then with density varying across sessions :
> AIC(Dsess, Dsess.sig0, Dsess.sig, Dsess.g0)
                                 model            detectfn npar    logLik       AIC       AICc      dAICc   AICcwt
Dsess.g0    D~session g0~h2 sigma~1 pmix~h2     halfnormal    7   -420.9591   855.918    861.813   0.000    0.4342
Dsess.sig   D~session g0~1 sigma~h2 pmix~h2     halfnormal    7   -421.2408   856.482    862.376   0.563    0.3277
Dsess        D~session g0~1 sigma~1 pmix~h2     halfnormal    6   -423.8593   859.719   863.919    2.106   0.1515
Dsess.sig0  D~session g0~h2 sigma~h2 pmix~h2   halfnormal    8   -420.5186   857.037    865.037   3.224   0.0866

Values of the parameters are consistent with the density constant or not, sigma and g0 higher for male, and the sex ratio is plausible.

Questions:
1/ Is it relevant to look for the best detection model first and to use it for the density modelling ? Should I try in the other way to see if there is any differences ?
2/ Should I model-average the first two model ? How to do it to then look for the best density parametrization ? Maybe fixing values of g0 and sigma, but I d'ont know how to do it for different sessions. Or should I choose the model with sigma and g0 modelled with the sex covariate because it seems logical to me despite the AIC ? How to justify it ? 
3/ Any remark or advise ?

Thank you
Yon

messages.author: 118cea91a1619106
messages.subject: Re: Sex covariate in multisession analysis
parts:
Hello Yon
I'm not expert in model selection, but for what it's worth:
1. First selecting a detection model, then selecting a density model, makes sense to me as a strategy when the model is large and slow (but I don't think you have that problem). I would do it with CL = TRUE to avoid assuming density constant. However, tThe log-likelihood and AICc differences are verging on trivial, and the AICc weights with and without constant density are very similar, so I don't see an issue.
2. Why average just the first two? Why not all?
But as I said I'm not the expert so won't engage in back and forth on this. Others may have ideas...
Murray

Hello Yon
I'm not expert in model selection, but for what it's worth:

Murray

Le mardi 29 juin 2021 à 22:17:42 UTC+2, murray...@gmail.com a écrit :
A multisession analysis allows you to fit a model with each detection parameter (g0 or lambda0 and sigma) held at the same value across years (e.g. g0~1, sigma~1). If that is a reasonable assumption (I expect it is) then there is no reason to 'lose' any data. It's worth also checking by AIC whether there is clear evidence for annual variation in density (D~session vs D~1). The 'heterogeneity' you see may just be sampling variation (although I expect not).
Murray

Yon,

I would not make a decision about selecting the best model or model averaging based solely on AIC values. There are other things to consider. Also, when estimating density you can oftentimes get very similar density estimates from models with very different AIC values. Is that the case here? If so, is it really that important to model average? 

I think you are on the right track with your questions, but I would consider AIC, parameter estimates and associated SEs (of both the model and resulting density estimates), and the biology/ecology of the species to make a decision about a best model or whether to model average.

Regards,

Duane

Le jeudi 16 décembre 2021 à 21:24:39 UTC+1, drd11 a écrit :
Yon,

I would not make a decision about selecting the best model or model averaging based solely on AIC values. There are other things to consider. Also, when estimating density you can oftentimes get very similar density estimates from models with very different AIC values. Is that the case here? If so, is it really that important to model average? 

I think you are on the right track with your questions, but I would consider AIC, parameter estimates and associated SEs (of both the model and resulting density estimates), and the biology/ecology of the species to make a decision about a best model or whether to model average.

Regards,

Duane

Le dimanche 7 novembre 2021 à 23:30:33 UTC+1, murray...@gmail.com a écrit :
Hello Yon
I'm not expert in model selection, but for what it's worth:
1. First selecting a detection model, then selecting a density model, makes sense to me as a strategy when the model is large and slow (but I don't think you have that problem). I would do it with CL = TRUE to avoid assuming density constant. However, tThe log-likelihood and AICc differences are verging on trivial, and the AICc weights with and without constant density are very similar, so I don't see an issue.
2. Why average just the first two? Why not all?
But as I said I'm not the expert so won't engage in back and forth on this. Others may have ideas...
Murray

Le mardi 29 juin 2021 à 22:17:42 UTC+2, murray...@gmail.com a écrit :
A multisession analysis allows you to fit a model with each detection parameter (g0 or lambda0 and sigma) held at the same value across years (e.g. g0~1, sigma~1). If that is a reasonable assumption (I expect it is) then there is no reason to 'lose' any data. It's worth also checking by AIC whether there is clear evidence for annual variation in density (D~session vs D~1). The 'heterogeneity' you see may just be sampling variation (although I expect not).
Murray
